Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
try hard not think about the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette: At forty-five, Dr. Prasit stood in a sweltering operating theater when a patient's drape caught fire. He watched helplessly as the anesthesiologist froze, the acrid scent of charred tissue filling his lungs while the skin on his forearm burned with a precise, 108-degree heat. The sheer stress of watching a life slip away while he could not stop the flames rewired his nervous system. Decades later, that specific temperature on the skin, the lingering stress of morning rounds, and the faintest whiff of a burnt smell do not merely remind him of the past; they violently pull him back into it. These sensory intrusions immediately spike his physiological alarm, making him jumpy and easily startled by any unexpected sound, like a dropped instrument or a sudden phone ringing in the hallway. Because his body keeps reacting as if he is still trapped in the flames, even when he is perfectly safe, Prasit has come to believe there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. This conviction of defectiveness tightens his constant vigilance, forcing him to walk through his days as if disaster is always one step away. The certainty that he is broken and the need to stay hyper-alert directly push him toward avoidance; he has learned to push away positive emotions because they feel profoundly unsafe, working to suppress any thoughts that drift toward the theater. This same belief in his own brokenness amplifies his threat response, turning ordinary auditory cues into perceived dangers and causing him to take excessive risks, such as driving at reckless speeds to outrun his panic. The conviction that he is defective also fractures his recall, making the memories of that night feel like they belong to someone else rather than to him, leaving him unable to put the events in the right order. The way he remembers the trauma directly fuels his avoidance habits. When the emotional intensity of the event floods him without any clear image, he feels compelled to suppress his thoughts and avoid watching television or reading about similar accidents, fearing the media will reopen the wound. This distorted recall also keeps his threat system chronically engaged; the confusion and alienation of his memories make him jumpy, heightening his startle response and pushing him toward risky behavior. Paradoxically, these fragmented, alien memories reinforce his original negative appraisals. He tells himself that because his mind cannot hold the event in a coherent sequence, his body must be an enemy, and his constant need for vigilance is the only thing keeping him alive. His physiological threat state directly dictates his coping strategies. The constant jumpy feeling and high alertness when he hears sudden noises make it impossible for him to relax, so he doubles down on his avoidance, deliberately isolating himself from positive experiences and suppressing the trauma from his consciousness. This hypervigilance and risky pacing also disrupt his memory processing. The relentless state of threat scrambles his cognitive integration, ensuring that the memories remain disjointed and emotionally overwhelming rather than properly contextualized. Conversely, his efforts to cope with the trauma only worsen his recall and sharpen his sensitivity to danger cues. By suppressing his thoughts and avoiding media, he starves his nervous system of natural resolution, which ensures the memories remain disjointed and emotionally overwhelming rather than properly contextualized. Avoiding positive feelings leaves his amygdala unchecked, meaning the temperature on his skin or a burnt smell now triggers an immediate, full-body alarm. Over decades, this loop has cost him his marriage and his clinical license; he now works in a quiet clinic, but the stress of any unexpected sound or sudden shift in air temperature still pulls him into the past. At seventy-seven, Prasit finally walks into a therapist's office because the relentless jumpy fear and alienating memories have made his daily life unbearable. What frightens him most is that he will never feel safe in his own skin again, and he hopes only to quiet the constant noise in his head.
